tips.title: Antigen is the marker, antibody is the weapon
tips.body: An **antigen** is a protein on the pathogen's surface. An **antibody** is made by a lymphocyte and is **complementary** in shape to that antigen, not the same shape as it.

tips.title: Memory cells, not antibodies, give immunity
tips.body: Antibodies break down after an infection. It is the **memory lymphocytes** that remain, which is why the second response is faster and larger. Saying antibodies stay for years is the common error.

tips.title: Vaccines use an inactive form of the pathogen
tips.body: A vaccine carries the pathogen's **antigens** in a form that triggers the immune response without causing the disease, so memory lymphocytes are made. The spec's word is **inactive**: dead, weakened or antigen-only vaccines all count. What matters is that it cannot cause the disease.

tips.title: Antigen, antibody, memory, in that order
tips.body: Immunity answers almost always run in the same sequence: the pathogen carries an **antigen**, lymphocytes make a **complementary antibody**, and **memory lymphocytes** remain. Writing those three in order gives the structure, and most mark schemes follow it line for line.

why.matters:
The body meets pathogens constantly and is ill rarely, which takes explaining. Most of the work is done by defences that are not clever at all — skin, mucus, stomach acid, lysozymes — and they stop nearly everything before it starts.

What is left goes to the **specific** immune system, and its remarkable property is not that it wins but that it **remembers**. Everything about vaccination follows from that one fact, and so does why you catch a cold every year and chickenpox once.

examples.title: Why you get chickenpox once and a cold every winter
examples.body:
The first time a pathogen arrives, the right lymphocyte has to be found and then multiply, which takes days — and you are ill while it happens. Afterwards the antibodies fade but the **memory lymphocytes** stay.

Meet the same pathogen again and the response is faster and far bigger: the pathogen is destroyed before it can make you ill. So why a cold every year? Because *the common cold* is hundreds of different viruses, and the ones that cause it change their surface **antigens** — so each time it is, to your immune system, a pathogen it has never met.

visual.alt: Two peaks of antibody concentration against time: a small slow rise the first time the pathogen is met, and a much larger and faster one the second time, which is why the second infection causes no illness

examples.title: Why a vaccine is the pathogen without the disease
examples.body:
A vaccine contains an **inactive** form of the pathogen — dead, weakened, or just the antigens from its surface. It cannot cause the disease, and that is the whole design.

What it can do is carry the **antigens**, and antigens are all the immune system ever responds to. So the body runs its slow first response against something harmless, and comes out of it with memory lymphocytes. The next meeting — with the real thing — gets the fast, large secondary response instead.

visual.alt: A flow chart of vaccination: an inactive pathogen is injected, its antigens are recognised, antibodies and then memory lymphocytes are made, and the real pathogen is destroyed quickly when it arrives

examples.title: Why your vaccination protects someone else
examples.body:
Some people cannot be vaccinated — babies too young for it, people whose immune systems are suppressed by treatment. They are protected anyway if enough of the people around them are, and that is **herd immunity**.

The mechanism is the route again: a pathogen that cannot find a new host stops spreading, so an unvaccinated person in a vaccinated population is unlikely ever to meet it. It also means the argument is not only about the person being vaccinated, which is why the specification asks you to **discuss** immunisation rather than to recommend it.

rows: herd immunity protects those who cannot

visual.alt: A table setting the case for immunisation against the case against it, for the person, for everyone else through herd immunity, and for the disease itself, which can be eradicated only if uptake stays high

steps.title: Keeping pathogens out
steps.body:
The first topic was about how pathogens spread. This one is about how the body stops them, and the first line of defence is simply keeping them out.

**Physical barriers** block the way in.
- **Skin** is a tough outer layer pathogens cannot get through. If it is cut, the blood clots and forms a scab to seal the gap.
- **Mucus** lines the nose and airways. It is sticky, so it traps pathogens that are breathed in.
- **Cilia** are tiny hairs on the cells lining the airways. They beat to waft the mucus, with its trapped pathogens, up to the throat, where it is swallowed.

Mucus and cilia work as a pair: one traps, the other removes.

rows: waft mucus up to be swallowed

steps.title: Chemical defences
steps.body:
Some pathogens get past the barriers, so the body also uses chemicals to kill them.

- **Lysozymes** are enzymes in tears, saliva and mucus. They break down the cell walls of bacteria, so the bacteria burst.
- **Hydrochloric acid** in the stomach kills most pathogens swallowed with food and drink, and those carried down in swallowed mucus.

That last point links back to the cilia: mucus is swallowed, so the pathogens trapped in it end up in the acid.

check.prompt: Name the acid in the stomach that kills pathogens.
check.solution: **Hydrochloric acid**. It makes the stomach contents strongly acidic, which kills most pathogens swallowed in food or drink before they can reach the intestines. This is a **non-specific** defence.

steps.title: Antigens, antibodies and lymphocytes
steps.body:
Pathogens that get past the barriers meet the **specific immune system**. Three words carry it.

- An **antigen** is a molecule, usually a protein, on the surface of a pathogen. Every kind of pathogen has its own antigens, with their own shape.
- **Lymphocytes** are a type of white blood cell. Each one has receptors that fit one particular antigen.
- **Antibodies** are proteins made by lymphocytes. Each has a shape **complementary** to one antigen, so it binds to that antigen and no other.

That is why it is called *specific*: an antibody against measles does nothing to flu. Once antibodies bind, the pathogens are destroyed, for example by being clumped together and engulfed by other white blood cells.

steps.title: The immune response, step by step
steps.body: The specification lists the response in stages, and the exam asks for them in order. The first time the body meets a pathogen, this is the **primary response**. It is slow — it takes days — which is why you feel ill while it builds.

visuals.problem: What happens when a new pathogen enters the body?

steps.text: The body is **exposed** to the pathogen
A lymphocyte with receptors complementary to its **antigen** recognises it
The new cells make **antibodies**, and some become **memory lymphocytes**
Antibodies bind to the antigens and the pathogens are destroyed

check.prompt: As well as antibodies, what else do antigens trigger the production of?
check.solution: **Memory lymphocytes**, which stay in the body and matter the next time.

markScheme.description: memory lymphocytes

options: lysozymes
memory lymphocytes
antibiotics

steps.title: Memory lymphocytes and the secondary response
steps.body:
After the infection, the antibodies gradually disappear. The **memory lymphocytes** do not; they stay in the blood for years.

If the same pathogen enters again, the memory lymphocytes recognise its antigen straight away. They divide quickly and antibodies are made. This **secondary response** is:
- **faster**: antibodies appear within a much shorter time;
- **larger**: many more antibodies are made.

So the pathogen is destroyed before it can multiply enough to cause symptoms. The person is **immune**.

The graph shows the shape of the two responses, each from the moment of exposure. There are no numbers because the point is the shape: the secondary curve rises sooner and higher.

visuals.alt: Two curves of antibody concentration against time after exposure: the second exposure peaks much sooner and much higher than the first

check.prompt: What stays in the body for years after an infection?
check.solution: **Memory lymphocytes** last; the antibodies from the first response fade away. That is the single most common mix-up in this topic.

markScheme.description: memory lymphocytes

options: the pathogen
memory lymphocytes
antibodies
antigens

steps.title: Immunisation
steps.body:
**Immunisation** (vaccination) gives the body its first meeting with a pathogen *without the disease*.

The vaccine contains an **inactive form of the pathogen**: dead, weakened, or just its antigens. It carries the antigens, so lymphocytes respond, but it cannot cause illness.

The antigens trigger a primary response: antibodies and, crucially, **memory lymphocytes**. If the live pathogen enters later, the memory lymphocytes give a fast, large secondary response and the pathogen is destroyed before symptoms develop.

So a vaccine does the same job as catching the disease, without the risk of catching it.

visuals.problem: How does a vaccine make someone immune?

steps.text: An **inactive** form of the pathogen is injected
Its **antigens** trigger lymphocytes to make antibodies and **memory lymphocytes**
steps.note: A primary response, with no illness

steps.text: Later, the live pathogen enters the body
Memory lymphocytes recognise the antigen: a **secondary response**
The pathogen is destroyed before symptoms develop

steps.title: For and against immunisation, and herd immunity
steps.body:
*(Biology only.)* The specification asks you to **discuss** immunisation, which means both sides.

**Herd immunity**: if a large proportion of a population is immunised, a pathogen cannot spread, because most of the people it could pass to are immune. That protects the people who *cannot* be immunised: babies too young for a vaccine, and people whose immune systems are weakened, for example by treatment for cancer.

**Advantages**
- Protects the individual from diseases that can kill or disable.
- Herd immunity protects others too.
- A disease can be wiped out altogether, as smallpox was.

**Disadvantages**
- Side effects: usually mild, such as a sore arm or a slight fever; very rarely a serious allergic reaction.
- Not everyone becomes immune, and some vaccines need **boosters**.
- Herd immunity fails if too few people take part.

steps.title: Your turn: why don't you get it twice?
steps.body:
Try this before reading the chain: *A person had measles as a child. Explain why they do not get measles again.* Aim for three linked points.

Then check your answer against the chain. The mark you are most likely to miss is the last one: it is not enough that the body *fights* the pathogen — it destroys it **before symptoms develop**.

steps.title: Going deeper: precise words, both differences
steps.body:
This topic rewards exact vocabulary more than almost any other.

**Complementary, not the same.** An antibody's shape is *complementary* to the antigen — it fits it, like a key and a lock.

**Memory lymphocytes, not antibodies.** Immunity lasts because memory lymphocytes last. Writing that *antibodies stay in the body* loses the mark.

**Both differences for the secondary response.** It is *faster* and *larger*. Most answers give one.

**Herd immunity is about spread.** Say *why* the unvaccinated are protected: the pathogen cannot pass through the immune people around them.

**New strains.** Flu changes its antigens, so last year's memory lymphocytes do not fit — a new vaccine is needed each year. That is the question they set to see who really understands *specific*.

visuals.alt: A table contrasting weak answers with grade 9 answers on immunity

check.prompt: A new strain of a virus appears. Why can't a vaccinated person's memory lymphocytes recognise it?
check.solution: The new strain's **antigens** are a different shape, so the memory lymphocytes are not complementary to them. Viruses have no cell wall, and antibodies belong to the host.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **Physical barriers**: skin (and scabs), mucus traps pathogens, cilia waft mucus up to be swallowed.
- **Chemical defences**: lysozymes in tears, saliva and mucus break down bacterial cell walls; hydrochloric acid in the stomach kills swallowed pathogens.
- **Antigen**: molecule on a pathogen. **Lymphocyte**: white blood cell. **Antibody**: protein complementary to one antigen.
- **Primary response**: the matching lymphocyte divides and makes antibodies and memory lymphocytes. It is slow, so you feel ill.
- **Secondary response**: memory lymphocytes recognise the antigen; antibodies are made **faster** and in **greater amounts**; the pathogen is destroyed before symptoms.
- **Immunisation**: an inactive form of the pathogen triggers a primary response without the disease.
- **Herd immunity**: when most people are immune the pathogen cannot spread, protecting those who cannot be immunised.
- **Against**: side effects, usually mild; not everyone becomes immune; some need boosters.

questions.prompt: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of immunisation. Include herd immunity in your answer.
questions.solution: A balanced answer. For: protects the individual from serious disease; if enough people are immunised, herd immunity protects those who cannot be (babies, people with weak immune systems); can wipe a disease out, as with smallpox. Against: side effects, usually mild (a sore arm, a fever) and rarely serious (an allergic reaction); does not always give immunity; some need boosters; some people cannot have them. Weigh them and conclude.

markScheme.description: Level 1 (1 to 2): an advantage or disadvantage stated
Level 2 (3 to 4): both sides, with herd immunity mentioned
Level 3 (5 to 6): both sides explained, herd immunity explained, and a conclusion

criteria.text: Advantages explained, such as protecting the individual and wiping out diseases
Herd immunity explained: unvaccinated people protected because the pathogen cannot spread
Disadvantages explained, and a reasoned conclusion

questions.modelAnswer: Immunisation protects the individual: memory lymphocytes mean that if the pathogen enters later, it is destroyed before it causes disease. It also protects other people. If a large proportion of a population is immunised, the pathogen cannot spread, because most of the people it could pass to are immune. This **herd immunity** protects people who cannot be immunised, such as young babies and people with weakened immune systems, and can remove a disease altogether, as happened with smallpox. On the other side, vaccines can have side effects: usually mild, such as a sore arm or a slight fever, but very occasionally a serious allergic reaction. They do not give every person immunity, some need booster doses, and some people cannot have them. Overall the advantages are much greater, because the side effects are usually mild and short-lived while the diseases prevented can kill; herd immunity only works if most people take part.

questions.prompt: Some people take a medicine that greatly reduces the amount of acid their stomach makes. Why might these people be more likely to get an infection from food?

questions.solution: **Less acid, so more pathogens survive.** The hydrochloric acid in the stomach is a chemical defence: it kills most of the pathogens swallowed with food and drink before they can reach the intestines. With far less acid, more of them survive the stomach and can cause infection. Acid has no part in making antibodies or mucus, and lysozymes in saliva work in the mouth, before the food reaches the stomach.

questions.prompt: A blood sample from an adult contains memory lymphocytes that recognise the antigens of the measles virus, but no antibodies against measles can be detected. Which statement is the best explanation?
questions.solution: **They met the antigen in the past and are immune.** After an infection or a vaccination, the antibodies gradually disappear from the blood, but the memory lymphocytes remain for years. If measles antigens enter again, those memory lymphocytes recognise them at once, divide rapidly and produce antibodies in a fast, large secondary response, so the person does not become ill. Immunity rests on the memory lymphocytes, not on antibodies staying in the blood. Memory lymphocytes are made only in response to an antigen, so nobody has them from birth, and they outlast the antibodies rather than disappearing with them.

questions.prompt: A medicine has a side effect of reducing the amount of tears the eyes produce. A patient taking it has repeated bacterial infections of the eyes, although blood tests show that the patient's white blood cells are normal. Which explanation is best?
questions.solution: **Tears contain lysozyme.** Lysozyme is an enzyme in tears that destroys bacteria by breaking down their cell walls, part of the body's chemical defences, along with the tears washing the surface of the eye. With fewer tears, more bacteria survive on the eye and can start an infection, even though the white blood cells of the specific immune system are working normally: that defence only comes into play once the pathogens are already in. The body does not make antibiotics, memory lymphocytes are not carried in tears, and tears are not acidic like the stomach.

questions.solution: **An antigen.** Antigens belong to the pathogen; antibodies are made by the body's lymphocytes and are complementary in shape to one particular antigen.

questions.prompt: In a trial of a new vaccine, 1600 children were given the vaccine. Blood tests later showed that 1552 of them had become immune to the disease. Calculate the percentage of the children who became immune.
questions.solution: $\dfrac{1552}{1600} \times 100 = 97$%. The other 3%, 48 children, did not become immune: not everyone responds to a vaccine, which is one of its disadvantages and one reason herd immunity matters.

markScheme.description: divides 1552 by 1600 and multiplies by 100

questions.prompt: A vaccine gives immunity to 96% of the people who receive it. For herd immunity against this disease, at least 84% of a population must be immune. A town has 60 000 people, of whom 48 000 have been vaccinated. Calculate how many more people must be vaccinated for the town to reach herd immunity.
questions.solution: Only 96% of those vaccinated become immune, so to make 84% of the population immune, the percentage vaccinated must be $\dfrac{84}{96} \times 100 = 87.5$%. For 60 000 people that is $0.875 \times 60\,000 = 52\,500$ vaccinated. The town has 48 000, so $52\,500 - 48\,000 = 4\,500$ more people must be vaccinated. (Another route: $0.84 \times 60\,000 = 50\,400$ must be immune and $0.96 \times 48\,000 = 46\,080$ already are, so $4\,320$ more immune people are needed, and $4\,320 \div 0.96 = 4\,500$.) Herd immunity protects the people who cannot be vaccinated and the 4% in whom the vaccine did not work, because a pathogen cannot spread when most of the people it could pass to are immune.

markScheme.description: divides 84 by 96 to find that 87.5% must be vaccinated, or finds that 50 400 must be immune and 46 080 already are
finds 87.5% of 60 000 = 52 500 and subtracts 48 000, or divides the shortfall of 4 320 by 0.96
4 500 people

questions.prompt: Some vaccines are given as two doses a few weeks apart. Explain why a second dose gives stronger and longer-lasting protection than a single dose.
questions.solution: The first dose contains an **inactive form of the pathogen**, whose antigens trigger lymphocytes to produce **antibodies** and **memory lymphocytes**; this primary response is slow and makes relatively few of each. When the second dose delivers the same antigens, the **memory lymphocytes recognise them** straight away, divide rapidly and produce antibodies **faster and in much larger amounts**, as in a secondary response. This second response also leaves behind **many more memory lymphocytes**, so if the real pathogen ever arrives the response is stronger and the protection lasts longer.

criteria.text: States that the antigens of the inactive pathogen in the first dose trigger a primary response in which some antibodies and some memory lymphocytes are made

questions.modelAnswer: A vaccine contains an inactive form of the pathogen, which still carries the pathogen's antigens. The first dose exposes the body to those antigens for the first time, so the lymphocytes respond slowly: over several days they produce antibodies complementary to the antigen, and some memory lymphocytes. The amounts are modest, which is why a single dose sometimes leaves a person only partly protected. When the second dose arrives a few weeks later, the antigens are already known. The memory lymphocytes recognise them at once, divide rapidly, and produce antibodies much faster and in far greater amounts, just as they would in a secondary response to the real pathogen. This larger response also produces many more memory lymphocytes, and those are what stay in the blood for years. So if the person later meets the real pathogen, there are more memory lymphocytes ready to respond, the pathogen is destroyed sooner, and the protection lasts longer than a single dose could give.

questions.prompt: A parent refuses a vaccine for their child, saying it is pointless because 5 in every 100 children who receive it do not become immune. Explain why the vaccine is still worth giving, both for this child and for other people.
questions.solution: For the child, the vaccine works in **95 out of 100** cases, so it is very likely to give immunity and makes the child far less likely to catch a disease that can kill or disable; a 5% failure rate is not a reason to accept a near-certain lack of protection. For others, every immune person helps build **herd immunity**: when a large enough proportion of the population is immune, the pathogen cannot spread, because most of the people it could pass to are immune. That protects the people who **cannot** be vaccinated, such as babies too young for the vaccine and people whose immune systems are weakened by cancer treatment, and it protects the 5% in whom the vaccine did not work, because they rarely meet the pathogen at all.

each immune person adds to herd immunity: with most people immune the pathogen cannot spread
this protects those who cannot be vaccinated and those in whom the vaccine failed, because they rarely meet the pathogen

questions.modelAnswer: The parent has turned a 95% success rate into a reason for refusing, which is the wrong way round. For the child, a vaccine that works in 95 out of every 100 children is very likely to produce the antibodies and memory lymphocytes that give immunity, so the child's chance of catching a disease that can kill or disable falls sharply. Without the vaccine that chance stays as high as it was. The vaccine also matters for people other than the child. When a large proportion of a population is immune, a pathogen cannot spread, because most of the people it could pass to are immune and the chain of infection breaks. This is herd immunity, and every vaccinated child adds to it. It protects the people who cannot be vaccinated at all, such as babies too young for the vaccine and people whose immune systems are weakened by treatment for cancer. It also protects the very children the parent is worried about: the 5 in 100 in whom the vaccine did not work are safe as long as the pathogen is not circulating around them. Refusing the vaccine weakens that protection for everyone, including this child if they turn out to be one of the 5.

questions.prompt: A person was exposed to a pathogen for the first time and was ill for about two weeks. Antibodies against it became detectable in their blood after 7 days, reached a peak of 15 arbitrary units on day 14, and had disappeared by day 50. On day 90 the person was exposed to the same pathogen again. Antibodies were detectable the next day, peaked at 240 arbitrary units on day 94, and the person had no symptoms. Explain the differences between the two responses, and explain how vaccination makes use of the same effect.
questions.skill: primary and secondary responses, and vaccination
questions.solution: **First exposure.** The pathogen's **antigens** are recognised as foreign and trigger an immune response: lymphocytes produce **antibodies** complementary to the antigen. Because the right lymphocytes are few and must multiply first, this primary response is **slow** (7 days before any antibody, a low peak of 15 units) and the person is ill while it builds. The antigens also trigger the production of **memory lymphocytes**, which remain in the blood after the antibodies have gone by day 50. **Second exposure.** The memory lymphocytes recognise the antigen at once and divide rapidly, so antibodies appear within a day and reach 240 units, **sixteen times** the first peak; the pathogen is destroyed before it can multiply enough to cause symptoms, so the person is **immune**. **Vaccination** injects an **inactive form of the pathogen**, which carries the same antigens but cannot cause the disease. This triggers the slow primary response and, crucially, the memory lymphocytes, so that a real infection later meets the fast, large secondary response instead of the slow primary one.

markScheme.description: Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): states that antibodies are made against the pathogen and that the second response is faster or larger, with little explanation of why

Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): explains that antigens trigger antibody production and memory lymphocytes in the first response, and that memory lymphocytes give the faster, larger second response, but the link to vaccination or to the absence of symptoms is thin

Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a full chain using the figures: slow primary response as lymphocytes are triggered by the antigens; memory lymphocytes made and persisting after antibodies fall; recognition and rapid division giving antibodies within a day and a sixteen-fold peak so the pathogen is destroyed before symptoms; and a vaccine's inactive pathogen providing the same antigens to create memory lymphocytes without illness

criteria.text: Says that on first exposure the pathogen's antigens are recognised as foreign and trigger lymphocytes to produce antibodies complementary to them

Explains that this primary response is slow and small (no antibodies for 7 days, a peak of only 15 units) because the lymphocytes have to be triggered and multiply first, so the person is ill meanwhile
Says that the antigens also trigger the production of memory lymphocytes, which stay in the blood after the antibodies have disappeared by day 50
Explains that on second exposure the memory lymphocytes recognise the antigen at once and divide rapidly, so antibodies appear within a day and reach a far higher peak, 240 units against 15
Explains that the pathogen is destroyed before it can multiply enough to cause symptoms, which is why the person is immune

Explains that a vaccine contains an inactive form of the pathogen carrying the same antigens, so it triggers the primary response and memory lymphocytes without causing the disease, and a real infection then meets the secondary response

questions.modelAnswer:
**The first response.** When the pathogen entered the body for the first time, the antigens on its surface were recognised as foreign. This triggered the specific immune system: the few lymphocytes able to make an antibody complementary to that antigen were activated and began to divide and produce antibodies. That takes time, which is why no antibody could be detected for 7 days and why the peak, on day 14, was only 15 units. During that week the pathogen was multiplying unchecked, so the person was ill. The antigens also triggered the production of memory lymphocytes. Once the infection was over the antibodies were broken down and had disappeared by day 50, but the memory lymphocytes stayed in the blood.

**The second response.** On day 90 the same antigens arrived again. This time the memory lymphocytes recognised them immediately and divided rapidly into antibody-producing cells, so antibodies were detectable within a day and the peak on day 94 was 240 units, sixteen times the first peak and reached in 4 days rather than 14. The pathogen was destroyed before it could multiply enough to damage cells, so there were no symptoms: the person was immune.

**How vaccination uses this.** A vaccine contains an inactive form of the pathogen, killed or weakened so that it cannot cause the disease, but still carrying the same antigens. Injecting it triggers the slow primary response, including the production of memory lymphocytes, while the person stays well. If the real pathogen ever arrives, it meets the fast, large secondary response rather than the slow primary one, exactly as on day 90, and the disease never develops. Vaccination gives a person the second response without having had the first illness.

examTechnique.body:
Immunity questions are mostly *explain* and *describe*, and they are marked on vocabulary. The difference between a mark and no mark is often a single word: *complementary*, *memory lymphocytes*, *before symptoms develop*. Learn the sequence of the immune response as a chain you can write in order, and practise it until the words come without thinking.

Immunisation is on the specification as *discuss*, which means both sides and a judgement. Herd immunity has to be explained, not just named: say that the pathogen cannot spread because most people are immune, so those who cannot be vaccinated are protected. The hardest questions change the context — a new flu strain, a smoker's damaged cilia — and ask you to apply the same ideas.
examinerErrors: Writing that antibodies stay in the body for years. It is the memory lymphocytes that remain.
Saying antibodies are *the same shape* as antigens, instead of *complementary* to them.
Giving only one difference for the secondary response. It is both faster and larger.
Stopping at *the body fights it off*, rather than saying the pathogen is destroyed before symptoms develop.
Naming herd immunity without explaining that the pathogen cannot spread through a mostly immune population.
Confusing antibodies with antibiotics. Antibodies are made by the body; antibiotics are drugs.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer uses the vocabulary exactly — antigen, lymphocyte, complementary antibody, memory lymphocyte — and writes the immune response as an ordered chain from exposure to destruction. It gives both differences in the secondary response and ends with the pathogen destroyed before symptoms. On immunisation it weighs both sides, explains herd immunity as a matter of spread, and concludes. It applies the same ideas to unfamiliar cases, such as why a new strain escapes a vaccine or why damaged cilia lead to infection.
